questions.prompt: After kernel bypass has removed everything it can from the receive path, what cost remains?
options: NIC internal latency, PCIe DMA, and the doorbell MMIO write — roughly 0.5–1 µs of irreducible hardware.
Only syscall entry and exit, roughly 50–200 ns, since every software layer above it has been deleted.
The `sk_buff` allocation, because the vendor driver still builds one before handing the frame to user space.
Interrupt delivery and the ISR, because no bypass technology can replace hardware interrupts with polling.
questions.explanation: Bypass deletes the interrupt, the `sk_buff`, protocol demux, the socket lock and queue, the wakeup, `copy_to_user`, and the syscall; what physics leaves behind is the NIC's own latency, the PCIe DMA, and the MMIO doorbell. The claim that only the syscall remains is the tempting one because the syscall is the most visible kernel artefact, but it is also the cheapest item on the list at 50–200 ns — the multi-microsecond costs were the interrupt and the wakeup. Nothing removes PCIe or the NIC's internal pipeline.

questions.prompt: Your business is graded on worst-case fill latency. Which statement best describes what bypass buys you over a tuned kernel?
options: The mean drops from ~5 µs to ~1 µs while p99.9 is unchanged, because tail events originate in the network fabric.
Mean and tail improve by the same factor of about four, because the removed costs are constant per packet.
p99.9 collapses from ~50 µs to ~2–3 µs, a roughly 25× tail win that dominates the roughly 4× mean win.
The tail only improves if you also deploy an FPGA; software bypass moves the median and nothing else.
questions.explanation: Bypass removes every scheduling decision from the data path, so the distribution collapses rather than merely shifting: median 5 µs / p99.9 50 µs becomes median 1 µs / p99.9 2–3 µs. The idea that mean and tail improve by the same factor is the seductive near-miss — it would be true if the removed costs were constant, but the wakeup and C-state exit are precisely the variable, occasional costs that build the tail. FPGA (~50–200 ns) is a further tier, not a prerequisite for tail improvement.

questions.prompt: With the kernel out of the data path, where does the guarantee "this process may only send from and receive into its own memory" come from?
options: From the kernel, which still validates each descriptor by trapping the doorbell MMIO write before the NIC reads it.
From an IOMMU, NIC-enforced per-VI filters, or SR-IOV virtual functions — or from nowhere, if the process is simply trusted.
From the PCIe root complex, which rejects any DMA that falls outside the process's mapped BAR window.
From NIC firmware, which walks the process's own page tables to resolve every DMA address it is given.
questions.explanation: Isolation has to be re-sourced from hardware once the kernel is gone: an IOMMU gives a per-device address space, Solarflare's per-VI hardware filter table stops a process receiving traffic it never legitimately bound, and SR-IOV partitions the device — and `uio_pci_generic` deployments simply grant raw access and trust the process. The suggestion that the kernel still validates descriptors at doorbell time is exactly what bypass abolishes: the doorbell is a plain store to an `mmap`ed BAR, with no trap and no syscall. Root is needed at setup, not per operation.

questions.prompt: What is the structural difference that makes `rte_mbuf` cheaper per packet than `sk_buff`?
options: A 232-byte header plus a separately allocated data page, but drawn from a lock-free ring rather than the slab allocator.
A refcounted, cloneable structure whose metadata spans 8–15 cache lines but which avoids the page-fragment allocator.
A 128-byte header pointing at a page-fragment buffer, so one allocation per packet instead of the kernel's two.
A 128-byte header immediately followed by headroom and data in one 2 KB mempool element — zero allocations per packet.
questions.explanation: Co-location is the whole trick: header, headroom and payload live in a single preallocated mempool element, so allocation is a pop from a per-lcore cache (~5 ns, no lock, no atomic) and the metadata occupies 1–2 cache lines instead of 8–15. The description of a 128-byte header pointing at a separate fragment is the closest miss — it gets the header size right but keeps the pointer chase and an allocation, which is precisely the `sk_buff` cost being removed. Cloneability and refcounting are `sk_buff` traits; `rte_mbuf` has a refcount only for fan-out.

questions.prompt: A feed handler cares only about the latency of one critical packet at a time. What does DPDK's burst-oriented API give it?
options: Little — bursting amortises the doorbell and enables prefetch pipelining, which is a throughput design, not a latency one.
A large win, because `rte_eth_rx_burst` blocks until the burst fills and thereby removes per-packet polling overhead.
A large win, because the burst size sets the RX descriptor ring depth and therefore raises the hardware drop threshold.
Nothing, because `rte_eth_rx_burst` is a syscall and so costs more per packet than an ordinary socket `recv` would.
questions.explanation: Bursting exists to amortise the doorbell write across many packets and to let you prefetch packet i+1's payload while handling packet i — both throughput optimisations that a one-packet-at-a-time consumer cannot exploit, which is why ef_vi and TCPDirect are leaner for this shape of workload. The claim that `rx_burst` is a syscall inverts the entire premise of DPDK: it is a plain function call that reads a cache line and occasionally writes a doorbell. Burst size is a call argument, unrelated to the configured ring depth.

questions.prompt: You run `dpdk-devbind.py --bind=vfio-pci` against the PCI address of the port carrying your SSH session. What happens?
options: The bind is refused, because the kernel will not detach a driver from an interface that has active TCP sessions on it.
The interface stays visible to `ip link` and `tcpdump`, but its statistics freeze for as long as a DPDK process holds it.
The kernel driver detaches, the interface vanishes from `ip link`, and you lose the box until someone unbinds it locally.
Traffic continues through the kernel path until an EAL process actually claims and configures the port at runtime.
questions.explanation: Binding to `vfio-pci` detaches the kernel driver immediately, at bind time, and the interface disappears from `ip link`, `ethtool` and `tcpdump` — this is why the standing advice is to use a separate NIC or port from your management interface. The idea that traffic keeps flowing until an EAL process claims the port is the most plausible wrong answer, since DPDK's userspace side does happen later; the detach, however, is a kernel operation that completes the moment the driver override is written. Nothing about active sockets blocks a driver unbind.

questions.prompt: Why does DPDK require huge pages?
options: Purely for TLB coverage — a 2 GB mbuf pool on 4 KB pages would miss the dTLB on essentially every packet.
Because `hugetlbfs` is the only mapping an IOMMU can program, so 4 KB pages cannot back DMA buffers at all.
Because a mempool's per-lcore cache must be one 1 GB allocation for its element indices to fit into 32 bits.
Primarily for physical contiguity and stable IOVA translation plus pinning; TLB coverage is real but secondary.
questions.explanation: The NIC DMAs to a bus address, so a 2 KB mbuf must not straddle into a discontiguous physical frame and the pages must be unswappable and unmigratable — a 1 GB `hugetlbfs` page satisfies contiguity and pinning at once, with `base_phys + offset` addressing. TLB coverage is the tempting single-cause answer because it is genuinely worth 50–150 ns per packet on a large pool, but it is a bonus rather than the requirement: a scattered, swappable pool is not merely slow, it is unusable for DMA. An IOMMU can map 4 KB pages perfectly well.

questions.prompt: A deployment script echoes into `nr_hugepages-1048576kB` after weeks of host uptime, gets fewer pages than requested, and EAL init then fails. What is the fix?
options: Reserve 1 GB pages on the kernel command line at boot; after uptime, physical memory is too fragmented to assemble them.
Switch to the `hugetlbfs` mount options, because the sysfs interface accepts only 2 MB requests and silently truncates 1 GB ones.
Raise `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` to unlimited, which is what caps the reservation and makes the runtime allocation succeed reliably.
Enable transparent huge pages first so the kernel's compaction daemon can assemble the gigabyte-sized physical blocks.
questions.explanation: A 1 GB page needs a gigabyte of contiguous physical memory, which only reliably exists early in boot — hence `default_hugepagesz=1G hugepagesz=1G hugepages=8` on the command line, and the characteristic signature of a silently short allocation followed by "Cannot get hugepage information". `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` is the most tempting distractor because it is a real DPDK prerequisite, but its failure signature is different: `VFIO_IOMMU_MAP_DMA` returning `ENOMEM` despite free memory. THP is irrelevant here and should generally be off, since its compaction is itself a jitter source.

questions.prompt: What is OpenOnload, architecturally?
options: A kernel module that shortens the receive path by skipping netfilter and routing for sockets marked as accelerated.
A full user-space TCP/UDP/IP stack `LD_PRELOAD`ed over the socket API, with transparent per-socket fallback to the kernel.
A raw-frame ring and event-queue API with no protocol stack, over which you implement UDP parsing yourself.
A burst-oriented poll-mode driver framework that detaches the NIC from its kernel driver when the port is bound.
questions.explanation: `libonload.so` interposes `socket`, `connect`, `recv`, `epoll_wait` and friends; sockets on an accelerated Solarflare interface run entirely in user space over a VI, and anything else falls through to the real syscall — which is why acceleration costs a launcher change rather than a rewrite. The raw-rings-with-no-protocol description is ef_vi, the layer Onload is itself built on; conflating the two is the standard mix-up. Onload is a user-space library, not a kernel module, and it does not detach the kernel driver the way DPDK's `vfio` bind does.

questions.prompt: You relaunch a UDP market-data receiver under `onload --profile=latency` and measured latency does not move at all. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Onload refuses to start when any socket cannot be accelerated, so the process would have exited with a diagnostic instead.
Onload accelerates a socket only after its first thousand packets, so short benchmark runs always measure the kernel path.
Acceleration applies only to TCP, so a UDP multicast receiver always runs at kernel speed regardless of the profile used.
The socket was never accelerated — wrong interface or an unsupported option — and silently fell back to the kernel path.
questions.explanation: Silent non-acceleration is Onload's classic failure mode: a socket bound to a non-Solarflare interface, or using raw sockets or an unsupported `setsockopt`/`SO_TIMESTAMPING` combination, quietly runs at kernel speed with no error anywhere, which is why `onload_stackdump lots` and `EF_LOG=all` are the habitual first check. The idea that Onload would refuse to start is the appealing wrong answer because it is what a well-behaved tool arguably should do — the transparent fallback is deliberate design, and it is exactly what makes the failure invisible. UDP multicast receive is in fact one of Onload's strongest paths.

questions.prompt: What does a single `ef_eventq_poll` call actually do when no packet has arrived?
options: It issues a PCIe read of the NIC's head-pointer register, costing roughly 300 ns even though nothing has arrived.
It scans the DD bits of every descriptor in the RX ring, so the idle cost scales with the configured ring depth.
It reads one 64-byte event-queue cache line and checks a phase bit — about 20–40 ns, no PCIe read, no syscall.
It performs a short `recvmmsg`-style syscall whose cost is about 200 ns thanks to the pre-mapped ring buffer.
questions.explanation: The NIC writes event descriptors into a separate event queue in host memory, each carrying a phase bit, so "is there a packet?" is one cache-line read with no device transition at all — this is why ef_vi's floor sits around 700–900 ns wire-to-application. Scanning descriptor DD bits is the tempting answer because that is how many ring designs work and how DPDK's PMD reads its ring, but the whole point of the separate event queue is to make the idle check a single fixed-cost read independent of ring depth. A PCIe read would cost hundreds of nanoseconds and is precisely what the design avoids.

questions.prompt: What does CTPIO do on the transmit path, and what does it cost?
options: PIO stores push the frame into the NIC's TX FIFO so transmission begins before the frame is complete; it burns PCIe bandwidth and suits only small frames.
It DMAs the frame from a pinned huge page while the descriptor is still being built, which saves the doorbell write for small frames.
It merges several RX events into a single completion so the poll loop reads fewer cache lines; it costs a little added receive latency.
It stages the frame in on-NIC SRAM at registration time so retransmits need no host access; it costs a block of pinned host memory.
questions.explanation: Cut-Through Programmed I/O writes the frame directly into the transmit FIFO with PIO stores instead of letting the NIC DMA-fetch it, so the wire begins moving before the whole frame has been written — sub-100 ns TX initiation, and the mechanism behind sub-microsecond tick-to-trade on non-FPGA hardware. The event-merging description is a real ef_vi feature (`EF_VI_RX_EVENT_MERGE`) but it belongs to the receive path, which makes it the easiest confusion. CTPIO's cost is inefficient PCIe utilisation, which is why it is restricted to small frames.

questions.prompt: A firm wants the lowest possible market-data receive latency, real TCP for order entry, and minimal engineering effort everywhere else. Which architecture fits?
options: ef_vi for both paths, since its raw-frame API ships a minimal TCP implementation suitable for exchange order-entry sessions.
DPDK for both paths, since its poll-mode driver beats ef_vi on one-packet latency and it ships a production TCP stack.
TCPDirect for both paths, since `zft_zc_recv` is the lowest-latency way available to receive UDP multicast market data.
ef_vi on the multicast receive fast path, Onload or TCPDirect for order entry, and the kernel for everything else.
questions.explanation: This hybrid is the idiomatic trading design: raw-frame ef_vi where you only parse UDP multicast and every nanosecond counts (~0.7–1.0 µs), a real TCP implementation where exchange interop and correctness matter, and the untouched kernel for management and everything non-critical. The TCPDirect-everywhere answer is tempting because TCPDirect genuinely does zero-copy receive and does handle UDP — but at ~0.8–1.2 µs it is not the lowest-latency receive path, ef_vi is. ef_vi supplies no protocol stack whatsoever, so it cannot cover order entry.

questions.prompt: What are the ownership semantics of TCPDirect's `zft_zc_recv`?
options: It returns a refcounted buffer whose lifetime you extend by cloning it, exactly as DPDK's mempool elements allow.
It hands back an `iovec` pointing into the receive ring; you parse in place and call `zft_zc_recv_done` to release it.
It copies the payload into a caller-supplied buffer while skipping the kernel, so no explicit release call is required.
It maps a fresh page per message with `mmap`, so releasing the data means calling `munmap` once parsing has finished.
questions.explanation: TCPDirect discards POSIX compatibility precisely so it can avoid the copy that `recv()` is obliged to make: the `iovec` points straight at the packet buffer in the ring, and ownership returns only when you call `zft_zc_recv_done`. The copy-into-your-buffer description is what Onload does — that is exactly the difference the `zf` API exists to eliminate, and confusing the two tiers is the common error. There is no cloning or refcount extension here; holding the `iovec` across many packets starves the ring and produces receive drops under load.

questions.prompt: One thread both runs strategy computation and calls `zf_reactor_perform`. Occasionally the strategy work takes 400 µs. What breaks?
options: Nothing on the TCP side: the NIC completes handshakes, ACKs and retransmissions in hardware for `zf` stacks.
Receive is unaffected because frames queue in the ring, but transmit stalls until the next `zft_send` flushes them.
The stack silently spawns a helper thread to service its timers whenever the reactor call is delayed beyond one RTT.
The reactor stops pumping, so ACKs, timers and retransmits stall — the peer retransmits and the session can time out.
questions.explanation: `zf_reactor_perform` is the pump for the entire stack — receive, TCP timers, retransmission and ACK generation — so a thread that stops calling it stalls the connection, and this coupling between application compute time and TCP correctness is the number-one surprise for teams that build or adopt reactor-driven stacks. The transmit-only answer is the most plausible miss because a stalled loop obviously delays sends, but it understates the damage: the peer's view of your ACKs is what actually breaks. There is no hidden helper thread; a `zf_stack` is single-threaded by design.

questions.prompt: Why does deploying VMA/XLIO purely for TCP and UDP acceleration still require the RDMA software stack (`rdma-core`, `libibverbs`, `libmlx5`)?
options: Because `libibverbs` supplies the `LD_PRELOAD` interposition machinery that VMA reuses to hook the socket symbols.
Because the verbs library owns the huge-page allocator VMA needs in order to back its packet pool with pinned memory.
Because VMA's user-space stack runs on an ibverbs raw-Ethernet queue pair with flow-steering rules and a polled CQ.
Because VMA turns every socket write into a one-sided RDMA write into the peer's pre-registered receive buffer.
questions.explanation: That layering is the notable architectural point about VMA/XLIO: rather than a proprietary VI API, it allocates a raw-Ethernet QP, registers memory regions, installs flow steering, and polls a completion queue — the RDMA software stack reused for plain Ethernet. The one-sided-write description is the seductive one because the verbs dependency invites the assumption that RDMA semantics are in play; in fact only the queue-pair plumbing is borrowed, and the wire protocol is ordinary TCP/UDP over Ethernet. `LD_PRELOAD` interposition is plain dynamic-linker behaviour and needs no verbs support.

questions.prompt: Where does an XDP program run in native mode?
options: In the driver, on the raw DMA'd frame, before any `sk_buff` has been allocated for the packet.
At `netif_receive_skb`, after `sk_buff` allocation but before protocol demultiplexing takes place.
In user space, over frames the driver has already redirected into a UMEM via the FILL ring.
On the NIC's own cores, which is why the eBPF verifier rejects programs containing unbounded loops.
questions.explanation: XDP is the earliest software hook in Linux — verified eBPF running inside the driver on the DMA'd buffer before allocation — which is what makes `XDP_DROP` cost only ~10–20 ns and scale to tens of Mpps per core for DDoS mitigation. The `netif_receive_skb` answer describes where `AF_PACKET` taps the path, and that is exactly the distinction between a tap and a pre-stack hook. Offloaded mode does run on a SmartNIC's cores, but it is one of three modes rather than the definition, and the verifier's loop restrictions apply regardless of mode.

questions.prompt: An AF_XDP receiver processes exactly 2048 packets and then goes permanently silent, with no error and no rising drop counter you can find. What is wrong?
options: The COMPLETION ring filled, so the kernel halted the receive path until outstanding TX descriptors were reaped.
The FILL ring was never refilled, so the driver ran out of empty UMEM frames and the drops carry no obvious counter.
The UMEM registration lapsed, because `XDP_ZEROCOPY` mode requires re-registering the region on every ring wrap.
The XDP program exhausted the verifier's instruction budget after 2048 invocations and was detached by the kernel.
questions.explanation: 2048 is the size of the initial fill, and that exact-count stall is the canonical signature: the FILL ring is how user space tells the driver "these frames are empty", and a program that never replenishes it leaves the driver with nowhere to put packets. The COMPLETION-ring answer is the closest miss because both rings are kernel-facing and both can stall you, but COMPLETION is the TX-side recycle path and does not gate receive. The verifier runs once at load time, not per invocation, and UMEM registration does not expire.

questions.prompt: Is `PACKET_MMAP` with `TPACKET_V3` a form of kernel bypass?
options: Yes — the ring is mapped into the process, so frames reach user space without the stack ever building an `sk_buff`.
Yes for receive but not transmit, because `PACKET_TX_RING` still traverses the qdisc layer for every frame it sends.
No — but it does skip `sk_buff` allocation, which is where the bulk of the kernel's per-packet receive cost lives.
No — the driver, NAPI and `sk_buff` allocation all still run; it removes `copy_to_user` and the per-packet syscall only.
questions.explanation: `AF_PACKET` taps the path at `netif_receive_skb`, so every kernel cost up to that point is still paid; `PACKET_MMAP` saves the copy and, once data is flowing, the syscalls — which is why it belongs on the capture and compliance path rather than the trading path. The answer that concedes it is not bypass but credits it with skipping `sk_buff` allocation is the sharpest trap: it reaches the right verdict through a false mechanism, and the skb is precisely what still gets built. `PACKET_QDISC_BYPASS` exists to skip the qdisc, so the transmit claim is wrong too.

questions.prompt: You need a hardware-timestamped compliance capture of all venue traffic, with no dedicated capture card and no perturbation of the trading path. What do you build?
options: A DPDK secondary process attached to the same port, reading the trading application's mbufs after it has freed them.
An `ef_vi` VI with a promiscuous filter on the trading interface, with buffers reposted by the strategy thread itself.
`TPACKET_V3` plus `PACKET_FANOUT` plus `SOF_TIMESTAMPING_RAW_HARDWARE`, running on housekeeping cores.
An `AF_XDP` socket in `XDP_ZEROCOPY` mode fed by an `XDP_REDIRECT` program attached to the trading queue.
questions.explanation: `AF_PACKET` hands you a *copy* while the packet still reaches the normal stack, `PACKET_FANOUT` scales the capture across cores by hash or CPU, and `PACKET_TIMESTAMP` with the raw-hardware flag puts PHC timestamps in the ring metadata — a tap, which is what a capture must be. The AF_XDP answer is the tempting modern-sounding one, but `XDP_REDIRECT` is a diversion rather than a tap: redirected frames never reach the stack, so you would be stealing the trading path's traffic rather than observing it. Reposting capture buffers from the strategy thread would put capture work on the hot path.

questions.prompt: Your firm is moving to bypass and must decide which protocol code to write in-house. What is the defensible split?
options: Buy TCP from a vendor and build UDP — market data is stateless receive-only multicast, a few hundred lines over ef_vi.
Build TCP and buy UDP — the vendor stacks add most of their value in multicast group management and reassembly.
Build both — an in-house stack removes the vendor's per-socket locking from every path the firm actually cares about.
Buy both — a UDP multicast receiver over ef_vi first requires reimplementing IGMP, ARP and IP reassembly correctly.
questions.explanation: TCP is where the correctness risk lives — timers coupled to your reactor, retention of sent data for retransmission, connection state on crash, and a decade of exchange interop testing you cannot replicate — while a UDP multicast receive path is single-direction and stateless. Building both is the tempting maximalist answer, and the locking complaint is even partly real, but it buys a few hundred nanoseconds in exchange for TCP bugs that manifest as silently duplicated or corrupted *orders*. Group membership and ARP are setup-time concerns handled by filters, not per-packet work you must reimplement.

questions.prompt: A team is writing a minimal in-house TCP inside a poll-loop architecture. Which difficulty most often surprises them?
options: Checksum offload is unavailable from user space, so every segment must be summed by the CPU at roughly 200 ns/KB.
Sequence arithmetic must move to 64 bits, because a colocated session wraps the 32-bit sequence space every hour.
The three-way handshake cannot complete without kernel assistance, so connection setup still costs a syscall per socket.
Timers run from your own reactor, so a long strategy computation delays ACKs and provokes retransmissions at the peer.
questions.explanation: Retransmission, delayed-ACK, keepalive and TIME_WAIT timers all have to be driven from the same loop that does strategy work, which couples application compute time directly to TCP correctness — the surprise being that a slow computation damages the *peer's* view of the connection, not just your own throughput. Sequence-space wrap is the most plausible-sounding distractor because 32-bit wrap is a genuine TCP concern, but it takes an enormous data rate to matter and an order-entry session is low-rate by construction. A user-space stack owns its handshake entirely; no syscall is involved.

questions.prompt: Beyond removing the wakeup, what does a pinned busy-poll loop buy you?
options: It holds the core in C0, keeps caches, TLBs and branch predictors warm, and holds the core's turbo frequency up.
It raises the thread's scheduling priority automatically, so the kernel will not preempt a core running at 100% use.
It lets the NIC coalesce interrupts more aggressively, because the driver observes the queue being drained promptly.
It keeps DDIO's write-allocate policy engaged, so incoming frames are DMA'd into L1 rather than into the last-level cache.
questions.explanation: The C-state point alone removes a 30–60 µs tail event, and a core that idles also drops frequency with a turbo ramp measured in tens of microseconds, loses its L1/L2 to whatever ran meanwhile, and re-enters through the scheduler. The DDIO answer is the most technically flavoured distractor: DDIO does place incoming data in the last-level cache, but that is a property of the platform's PCIe write policy and has nothing to do with whether your thread is spinning. Busy-polling confers no scheduling priority — that is what `SCHED_FIFO` is for.

questions.prompt: What is the specific hazard of running a `SCHED_FIFO` busy-poll loop on a core that is not in `isolcpus`?
options: The kernel demotes the thread to `SCHED_OTHER` once it exceeds its slice, so latency silently regresses over time.
`SCHED_FIFO` threads cannot be pinned with `sched_setaffinity`, so the loop migrates and repeatedly loses warm caches.
Real-time priority disables `PAUSE` hinting on that core, roughly doubling the power drawn by the empty branch.
A loop with a bug that never yields can wedge the whole machine; `sched_rt_runtime_us` is the only safety valve.
questions.explanation: A `SCHED_FIFO` thread outranks everything, so a spin that never blocks starves kernel threads and your own shell on that core; the RT throttler configured by `sched_rt_runtime_us` is what keeps a mistake recoverable. The demotion story is the appealing wrong answer because it describes how a well-behaved system arguably ought to defend itself — Linux does not do this for `SCHED_FIFO`, which is precisely why the throttler exists as a separate mechanism. `sched_setaffinity` works normally for real-time threads, and `PAUSE` is a plain instruction hint unaffected by scheduling class.

questions.prompt: Zero-copy receive removes `copy_to_user`. What is the dominant part of the saving?
options: The copy itself, at 600–1000 ns per frame, which dominates every other cost remaining on the receive path.
Avoided cache pollution plus one fewer serial pass over the data; the copy itself is only 60–100 ns per frame.
The allocation of the destination buffer, a slab allocation costing about 300 ns even inside bypass stacks.
The TLB shootdown that `copy_to_user` performs on the receiving core before it may touch the user's page.
questions.explanation: A copy reads 24 cache lines and writes 24 more, and under DDIO the source is already in L3, so the copy drags it into L1 and evicts a chunk of your order book — while parse-in-place touches only the lines you actually read, often just the first 64 bytes, and makes the first field available a serial pass earlier. Overstating the raw copy cost is the natural error: it is real but undramatic at 60–100 ns for a full frame. TLB shootdown belongs to `TCP_ZEROCOPY_RECEIVE`, whose per-receive `mmap`/`munmap` cost is exactly why it is useless for market data.

questions.prompt: Under load only, later fields of large messages intermittently contain garbage; the earlier fields are always fine, it never reproduces under a debugger, and ASan reports nothing. What is happening?
options: Buffers are held too long, so the ring starves and the hardware drops frames without incrementing any software counter.
The completion ring is read out of order, so `wr_id` values end up matched against the wrong receive buffers entirely.
A receive buffer is being reposted before the parse has finished, so the NIC overwrites it partway through the read.
The doorbell store is missing its fence, so the device reads a stale descriptor and re-uses a previously freed address.
questions.explanation: Reposting hands ownership back to the device, and the next inbound frame overwrites the buffer while you are still walking it — corruption therefore appears only in the fields you had not yet read, only when traffic is dense enough to reuse the buffer quickly, and invisibly to ASan because the writer is a *device*. Holding buffers too long is the other genuine failure of this ownership contract and the most tempting answer, but its signature is drops with a rising hardware counter and no corruption at all. A missing doorbell fence hangs the queue silently rather than corrupting payloads.

questions.prompt: Why is a per-entry phase bit preferable to a device-written producer index for a polled completion ring?
options: The device writes a producer index into a dedicated cache line, which the poller reads before touching any ring entry.
The application issues a PCIe read of the device's tail register, which is why idle polling costs roughly 300 ns.
A generation counter lives in the doorbell register, so each poll amounts to a single uncached MMIO load.
Each entry carries a bit that flips on wrap, so polling is one cache-line read with no separate index to fetch.
questions.explanation: With a phase bit, checking for work is "read the next entry's cache line; if its phase matches the expected generation, it is new" — one read, no PCIe transaction, no extra synchronisation, which is why `ef_eventq_poll` lands around 20 ns. The producer-index design is the closest miss because it is genuinely used (`io_uring`, AF_XDP) and is perfectly correct; it simply costs the device an extra cache line write and the poller an extra read on every check. Anything involving an MMIO or PCIe read on the idle path defeats the purpose entirely.

questions.prompt: x86-64 is TSO, so stores are never reordered with stores. Why is a compiler barrier still not enough between the descriptor writes and the doorbell write?
options: The doorbell usually lands in a write-combining region, and WC stores are weakly ordered and buffered — an `SFENCE` is needed.
TSO permits store-store reordering across MMIO addresses specifically, so a hardware fence is required for any device write.
Descriptor stores are non-temporal by default in DPDK and ef_vi, so they bypass the store buffer and can arrive late.
The IOMMU may reorder the device's DMA reads relative to the doorbell unless an `MFENCE` drains its translation queue.
questions.explanation: TSO does order the descriptor stores among themselves, but the doorbell is typically mapped write-combining, and WC stores sit in a buffer with weak ordering — without an `SFENCE` (or a release fence) the write may not leave the CPU promptly or in the right order, and the failure mode is a silent hang with no error anywhere. The claim that TSO carves out an exception for MMIO addresses is the plausible-sounding inversion: the memory type, not the address being MMIO, is what relaxes the ordering. On ARM this is unconditional and a `DMB ISHST` or `DSB` is mandatory.

questions.prompt: You are writing the completion handler for a multi-queue bypass path. How should each completion be matched back to its buffer?
options: By ring position, which is safe because a single queue pair always completes work requests in submission order.
By the buffer's DMA address, which the device echoes back inside every completion regardless of the transport used.
By a monotonically increasing sequence held in the completion's phase bits, which the device assigns at post time.
By the `wr_id` carried in the completion — never by position, since some transports and paths complete out of order.
questions.explanation: RDMA's unreliable transports and various multi-queue paths genuinely complete out of order, so the work-request ID you chose at post time is the only reliable key; matching by position silently pairs a completion with the wrong buffer and produces a double free or corruption on the next reuse. Position-matching is tempting because a single RC queue pair usually does complete in order — the inference breaks because "usually, on this transport" is not a contract, and the code outlives the transport choice. The phase bit signals newness, not identity.

questions.prompt: An architect proposes running RDMA to the exchange to shorten the venue-facing path. What is the correct objection?
options: Exchange gateways speak RoCEv2 but only over an InfiniBand link layer, which a colocation cross-connect cannot carry.
One-sided writes would let the venue read the firm's order book directly, which market regulators explicitly prohibit.
RDMA's ~15 µs one-way latency is worse than a tuned kernel TCP path, so there is nothing to gain at the boundary.
Venues deliver plain Ethernet UDP and TCP, RDMA's lossless-fabric requirements do not survive a cross-connect, and its trust model is intra-firm.
questions.explanation: There is simply no RDMA on the venue side, so it cannot shorten wire-to-strategy at all; on top of that, PFC/DCB or a subnet manager cannot be negotiated across an organisational boundary, and the `rkey` capability model assumes a trusted fabric. The latency objection is the most tempting because it sounds quantitative, but it inverts the real numbers — RDMA write latency is ~1–2 µs against roughly 15 µs for a kernel TCP round trip, so RDMA is fast; it is just inapplicable here. RDMA's proper home is internal replication and fan-out.

questions.prompt: What does `ibv_reg_mr` actually do, and roughly what does it cost?
options: Copies the buffer into a bounce region on the HCA and returns a handle to it — a few microseconds per call.
Allocates the protection domain and queue pair the region will be used with, then maps the doorbell page in.
Pins the pages, builds the NIC's translation tables, and issues an `lkey` and an `rkey` — tens to hundreds of µs.
Marks the pages `MADV_DONTFORK` and installs an `mmu_notifier`, leaving address translation to the IOMMU at runtime.
questions.explanation: Registration does three things at once — `get_user_pages` pinning charged against `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`, MTT/MPT population so the NIC can translate a virtual address in a work request, and key issuance where `lkey` authorises local access and `rkey` is a remote capability — and the per-page work plus device command is why it costs tens to hundreds of microseconds and belongs at startup. The `MADV_DONTFORK` answer is a real mechanism but describes `ibv_fork_init()`, a separate call, and it omits pinning and translation entirely. No data is copied to the HCA.

questions.prompt: A process registers a large memory region, then later forks a logging child. Corruption starts appearing in the parent's buffers. What is the mechanism?
options: Copy-on-write can leave the NIC DMAing to a physical page the parent no longer owns; `ibv_fork_init()` must precede registration.
The child inherits the `lkey`, so both processes post work requests against the same queue pair and interleave their data.
Registered memory is not inherited across `fork` at all, so the parent's pointers into the region go stale once the child exits.
The child's `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` accounting double-charges the region, so every subsequent registration fails with `ENOMEM`.
questions.explanation: COW can hand the *child* the original physical page and give the parent a fresh copy, while the NIC keeps DMAing to the original physical address it recorded at registration time — silent DMA into the wrong process's memory. `ibv_fork_init()` fixes this by `madvise(MADV_DONTFORK)`ing registered regions, and it must be called before any registration, which is the part people get wrong. The `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` answer names a real constraint but the wrong failure: exceeding the limit produces a clean `ENOMEM` at registration, not corruption of already-working buffers.

questions.prompt: A vendor suggests On-Demand Paging to eliminate registration cost on your order-entry latency path. How do you respond?
options: Accept — ODP faults all pages in at queue-pair creation, so the hot path still sees fully pinned memory with no setup cost.
Accept — ODP is mandatory whenever the region is backed by 1 GB huge pages, which a trading arena always is in practice.
Reject — ODP is incompatible with `IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_WRITE`, so one-sided replication cannot make any use of it at all.
Reject for a latency path — ODP trades registration cost for an unbounded first-touch page-fault latency at runtime.
questions.explanation: ODP lets the NIC page-fault through the kernel instead of requiring pinning, which removes both the registration cost and the pinning limit — but a page fault on the hot path is exactly the unbounded stall a latency system exists to eliminate, so it is fine for bulk transfer and fatal here. The claim that ODP pre-faults at QP creation is the tempting one because it would make the feature free; the whole mechanism is that faults happen on demand, hence the name. Huge pages are an independent optimisation that reduce MTT entries, not an ODP prerequisite.

questions.prompt: Which statement about RDMA queue-pair transport types is correct?
options: UD supports one-sided WRITE but not READ, because a write needs no return path from the target's adapter.
One-sided READ and WRITE require RC (or UC); UD is connectionless send/recv only, capped at one MTU per message.
All four transport types support one-sided operations; RC merely adds hardware retransmission on top of them.
One-sided operations require UD, because a connected transport must consume a receive WQE at the target host.
questions.explanation: One-sided operations address remote memory through a connection's established context, which is why they need RC or UC; UD behaves like UDP — one queue pair talking to many peers, send/recv only, one MTU per message — and is used for multicast and discovery. "UD supports WRITE but not READ" is the sharpest distractor because the reasoning sounds right (a write is fire-and-forget), but UD supports neither. RC is the default choice precisely because it gives hardware ACKs, ordering, and the full operation set, at the cost of N² queue pairs at scale.

questions.prompt: Your order messages are 48 bytes. Why set `IBV_SEND_INLINE` on the send work request?
options: The payload is copied into a bounce buffer on the HCA, so the send buffer may be reused at once without a completion.
The send completes without consuming a receive WQE at the target, which removes the RNR-retry risk for small messages.
The message skips the send queue entirely and is written through the doorbell register as immediate data instead.
The payload is embedded in the WQE itself, so the NIC needs no second DMA read to fetch it — several hundred ns saved.
questions.explanation: Without inlining, the NIC must issue a separate DMA read to fetch the payload after reading the WQE; embedding a small payload (device-specific, typically ≤64–256 bytes) removes that round trip for roughly 300–600 ns, which is exactly the message-size regime a trading system lives in. The bounce-buffer answer is tempting because early buffer reuse is a genuine side benefit of inlining, but it misdescribes the mechanism — the data goes into the work queue entry, not into HCA-side storage. Receive-WQE consumption is a property of SEND versus RDMA WRITE, unrelated to inlining.

questions.prompt: To cut polling work, an engineer marks every send unsignalled. Soon `ibv_post_send` starts returning `ENOMEM`. Why?
options: Unsignalled sends never free their send-queue slots, so the queue fills — signal every Nth send to bound outstanding work.
Unsignalled sends still consume completion-queue entries, so the CQ overruns and drives the queue pair into its error state.
Unsignalled sends are legal only on UD queue pairs, so an RC send queue begins rejecting them once its ring first wraps.
Unsignalled sends disable hardware retransmission, so unacknowledged segments pile up in the retransmit buffer until it fills.
questions.explanation: Completions are what let you reclaim send-queue WQEs, so suppressing all of them means the queue monotonically fills until posting fails — the standard practice is to signal every Nth send, often enough to keep the queue draining while still saving most of the CQ bandwidth and polling work. The CQ-overrun answer is the most plausible miss because CQ overrun is a real and worse failure (it transitions the QP to `IBV_QPS_ERR` with a cascade of `WR_FLUSH_ERR`), but unsignalled sends generate no CQ entries at all, so it cannot be the cause here.

questions.prompt: A team registers its entire heap as one memory region at startup and hands the resulting `rkey` to each peer. What is the exposure?
options: The HCA confines remote access to sub-ranges named in prior work requests, so the exposure is bounded in practice.
The `rkey` expires when the queue pair leaves RTS, so exposure lasts only as long as the connection itself lasts.
Any peer holding the `rkey` can read or write the whole heap, with no CPU involvement and no audit trail on your side.
The protection domain confines each peer to regions it has itself registered, so cross-process exposure cannot arise.
questions.explanation: The `rkey` is a 32-bit capability token with no per-operation authorisation, no logging and no revocation, so possession plus a virtual address is total access to the region — which is exactly why the discipline is to register minimal, purpose-built regions per peer or to use type-2 memory windows that rebind cheaply on the fast path. The protection-domain answer is the most tempting because a PD *is* the local isolation boundary, grouping MRs and QPs that may be used together; it constrains your own objects, not what a remote holder of a valid `rkey` may touch.

questions.prompt: You must replicate an order book to a hot standby while spending zero CPU on the standby. Which RDMA shape fits?
options: Two-sided SEND/RECV backed by an SRQ — the standby posts receives once and the hardware refills the queue for it.
One-sided RDMA READ issued by the primary, which pushes the book into the standby without paying a round trip.
RDMA ATOMIC fetch-and-add per update, the only operation whose ordering against the target's own CPU is guaranteed.
One-sided RDMA WRITE — the standby's CPU is never involved, interrupted or notified, which is the entire point.
questions.explanation: A one-sided WRITE lands bytes in the target's memory with no completion, no interrupt and no thread on the receive side, so replication is genuinely free for the standby and failover finds the state already present. The SRQ answer is the strongest distractor because a shared receive queue really does reduce buffer pre-posting across many connections — but SEND/RECV is two-sided by definition: the standby must have posted receive WQEs and gets a completion for every message, which is precisely the CPU cost being eliminated. A READ fetches rather than pushes and costs a full round trip.

questions.prompt: A design signals arrival by placing a flag at the end of the payload and sending the whole thing as one large RDMA WRITE. What is wrong with it?
options: It is safe on RC, because RC guarantees byte-ordered delivery within a single work request on all conforming hardware.
A single large write is not guaranteed to land in address order, so the flag can become visible before the payload does.
It is unsafe only on UC, since RC's hardware ACK forces the entire payload to be visible before any part of it is readable.
It is safe provided the flag is 64-bit aligned, because the adapter is specified to write naturally aligned words last.
questions.explanation: RDMA orders operations against each other on the same RC queue pair, but it says nothing about the internal landing order of the bytes within one write, so an in-band trailing flag is not safe on all hardware. The safe constructions are two separate WRITEs on the same RC QP, `IBV_WR_RDMA_WRITE_WITH_IMM` (which consumes a receive WQE and delivers a 32-bit tag in a completion), or a seqlock-style version pair. The "RC guarantees it" answer is the standard trap: RC's reliability and ordering guarantees are real, but they operate between work requests, not within one.

questions.prompt: Why is RoCEv2 operationally harder to run than InfiniBand?
options: RoCEv2 is not routable, so PFC is required simply to carry its IB link layer across subnet boundaries at all.
RoCEv2 runs over TCP, so its congestion control fights the switch's ECN marking and needs DCQCN to arbitrate.
Each RNIC must run a subnet manager in firmware, and `opensm` conflicts with standard Ethernet DCB settings.
The IB transport assumes losslessness and answers loss with go-back-N, so the Ethernet fabric needs PFC plus ECN/DCQCN.
questions.explanation: RoCEv2 encapsulates the IB transport in UDP/IP over Ethernet, and that transport reacts to a drop with go-back-N retransmission, which at scale collapses throughput — so the fabric must be made artificially lossless with Priority Flow Control plus ECN/DCQCN, and PFC brings deadlock, congestion spreading and pause storms. The TCP answer describes iWARP, not RoCE, and is the easiest of the three to mistake for the truth. RoCEv2 is explicitly routable (UDP destination port 4791), and the subnet manager belongs to native InfiniBand.
